articles.title: How to Rob a Bank review – Amazon’s anti-capitalist caper is far from a riot
articles.summary: Nicholas Hoult, Anna Sawai and Pete Davidson play Robin Hood in this simple-minded and unexciting attempt to mix social commentary with action. In case you were somehow blissfully unaware, America is in a very dark place and Americans are not very happy about it.
body: It’s therefore theoretically ideal timing for films that provide some sort of rousing David v Goliath catharsis, a win on-screen when one feels entirely out of reach in real life. But like Paul Greengrass’s muddy and muddled peasant revolt drama The Uprising which crashed and burned in September, David Leitch’s How to Rob a Bank can’t quite find a way to capture a moment that should be easy to capture. The director is best known for synthetic action films that prioritise noise above all else, from Deadpool 2 to Bullet Train to Hobbs & Shaw, a tonal through-line that could be most generously described as “annoying”.

articles.title: Prima Facie review – Cynthia Erivo’s brilliant barrister blazes in sexual assault drama
articles.summary: Adaptation of the international stage hit stars a commanding Erivo as Tessa, whose career defending rape suspects is undermined by experience. A blazingly fierce, effortlessly commanding central performance from Cynthia Erivo, like something from classical drama, powers this movie adaptation of…
body: In the theatre, it is a bravura solo spectacle, a stream-of-consciousness torrent which puts you right inside the trauma and the terror. The movie opens things out to a more conventionally presented drama and we lose something of that overwhelming moment-by-moment access to the lead character’s inner thoughts. But the resulting story is robustly constructed and tremendously acted.

The title is a legal Latin term meaning “on the face of it”, applied to evidence which appears, perhaps wrongly, to clinch a certain case, and the film leaves it up to us to decide how that is relevant here. Erivo plays Tessa Ensler, a brilliant young barrister who has battled racism and classism to get where she is, relishing her mastery of cross-examination and in love with the theatre and spectacle of the law. But without quite admitting it to herself, she has made her name defending men who need women to defend them for the optics in rape cases, and she is ruthless and cunning in undermining female complainants in the witness box.

articles.title: Irma P. Hall, ‘Soul Food’ and ‘The Ladykillers’ Actress, Dies at 91
articles.summary: Irma P. Hall, who played Josephine “Big Mama” Joseph in the 1997 dramedy “Soul Food,” died on Tuesday, her family confirmed. She was 91. “Irma P. Hall was a beloved actress, author, poet, educator and public speaker whose contributions touched countless lives throughout her remarkable career,” her…
body: Born in Beaumont, Texas, Hall was raised in Chicago before graduating from Texas College in 1956. She became a high school teacher and taught French, Spanish and other languages in Houston and Dallas until she began acting full time in 1984.

Her first role was as Georgia Brown in the independent film “Book of Numbers,” directed by Raymond St. Jacques. She was performing a poem when he scouted her and offered her the role on the spot. She instantly discovered her love for acting. She went on to act in several films and TV shows, including Ron Howard’s action thriller “Backdraft” in 1991 and Peter Macdonald’s comedy-drama “Mo’ Money” in 1992.
Her career continued to grow with “Family Thing,” “Nothing to Lose” and “Steel” before she landed the role of Big Mama.

She received the NAACP Image Award for Outstanding Supporting Actress in a Motion Picture in 1998. “Soul Food” was a hit at the box office, prompting the spinoff series “Soul Food: The Series,” where Hall reprised her role in fantasy sequences.

articles.title: Geese’s Soaring Live Show Lives Up to the Hype, With Fearless Improvisations and Boundless Energy: Concert Review
articles.summary: There are reasons why people are so excited about Geese, the most exciting rock band to emerge from New York in decades. It’s the buzz that envelops a band in the middle of an ascent, as its most recent record “Getting Killed” was passionately received by critics and fans alike.
body: The first surprise of the Geese live experience is Green’s swagger and experimentation. The guitarist is a key player in guiding the band’s more experimental moments and ferocious improvisation. Often tinkering with pedals as her fingers fly across the fretboard, she’s able to stretch a song to the outer limits, only to snap back quickly and clearly when a sharp riff is called for. Bassin also is central to the style, furiously playing all over his kit while still keeping in the pocket, ready to let loose during solos on songs such as the jumpy kiss-off “Bow Down.” DiGesu’s bass was often the steadiest instrument of the night, deep and powerful despite flights of fancy from his bandmates.

articles.title: FKA Twigs Becomes Josephine Baker: Inside the Lavish, Globe-Spanning Biopic from Maimouna Doucouré and Studiocanal (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.summary: On a crisp October afternoon in the Bois de Vincennes, on the outskirts of Paris, FKA twigs is transported back to 1950s America. Wearing a cream-colored pinstriped coat, a dark beret and black leather gloves, the British singer and dancer has been up since the early hours, with a 4 a.m.
body: Between takes, FKA twigs stays in character, looking pensive and emotional. The atmosphere on set is studious and distinctly international, with cast and crew switching between English and French.

And while the cemetery scene unfolding that afternoon is intimate, other sequences have the scale and flamboyance of a classic Hollywood production, notably those recreating the legendary Folies Bergère cabaret in Paris, where Baker became a sensation in the 1920s. The sprawling production has enlisted some 2,400 extras.

Yet behind the lavish costumes, musical performances and sweeping historical canvas, “Josephine Baker” is ultimately a portrait of a woman whose extraordinary public life was shaped by private wounds.

“What’s most important to me is not simply portraying Josephine as this powerful woman, this icon who was inducted into the Panthéon. We already know that side of her. I want to tell the story of the woman behind the icon,” says Doucouré, the Sundance-winning filmmaker behind “Cuties” and “Hawa,” speaking during lunch with the crew.

articles.title: Give Me the Ball! review – tennis trailblazer Billie Jean King is ferocious force for equality
articles.summary: Sparky and engaging documentary about the ‘battle of the sexes’ player, who fought her whole career to ensure the women’s game got the respect it deserved. After the engaging Evert and Navratilova documentary Chris and Martina: The Final Set comes this watchable and engaging documentary portrait of…
body: King (née Moffitt) was a ferocious force in women’s tennis from the 60s onwards and a vehement but polite advocate for equal rights on prize money. The women’s game was equally skilful, though not possessed of the same brutal brawn-power, and sold as many stadium seats. King sensationally helped to launch the Virginia Slims women’s tour – one of the great commercial revolutions in US sports, and had to work hard on promotion and sponsorship at the same time as simply training and playing. And while all this was happening, she had to come to terms with her gay sexuality, while married to the poignantly devoted Larry King, who is a gallantly supportive interviewee here.

In the 80s, King was put through another ordeal when her vengeful ex-partner Marilyn Barnett sued for “galimony”, thus revealing King’s sexuality to the world, which again she had to face out at a press conference in the company of her husband and bewildered parents. This is an enjoyable film, though I was surprised that no male tennis player could be found to praise King’s importance, not even the otherwise ubiquitous John McEnroe.

articles.title: Female Perversions review – Tilda Swinton searches for erotic adventures in rework of Madame Bovary
articles.summary: The actor’s 1996 first US film, as a lawyer trying to manage her complicated love life and traumatic fantasies, marked her out as a screen presence like no other. Tilda Swinton made her US debut 30 years ago with this insouciant, startling, experimental adventure in eroticism and neuroticism.
body: Streitfeld’s fictional reworking does not focus on Emma Bovary. Instead Swinton plays a character called Eve, a brilliant, beautiful – and single – lawyer with an elegant, angular style; she is as graceful and sometimes comically clumsy as a baby giraffe. Eve is having a passionate affair with a hunky seismologist called John (Clancy Brown), an amusing metaphor for the quake-level sex they’re having. She is also deeply attractive and attracted to women, yet also assailed by traumatised fantasies or flashbacks of something in her past; there are terrible lurches of guilt or fear, abuse, loss, self-harm or impostor syndrome.

articles.title: Toby Jones stars in film about UK Mars mission
articles.summary: Mackenzie Crook directs the story of the British professor whose probe lost contact upon touchdown.
body: Bafta-winning actors Toby Jones and Emily Watson have finished work on a film about the scientist behind Britain's first spacecraft to land on Mars, which got "lost".
Mars Express, directed by Mackenzie Crook, will see Jones play Colin Pillinger while Watson is his wife Judith.

The couple began developing the unmanned Beagle 2 probe to search for life on Mars while Pillinger was a professor of planetary sciences at the Open University in Milton Keynes. The probe went out of contact upon landing in December 2003, until it was finally spotted in 2015, after Pillinger died.
Crook said: "It's a complete honour to be telling the extraordinary story... for my first feature film as director."

body: Gavin and Stacey star Joanna Page has confirmed she will appear on the upcoming reality TV series I'm a Celebrity, with her former co-star Ruth Jones urging her to "have a crackin' time".
Page, who played Stacey Shipman in the BBC comedy, is joining this year's line-up of celebrities on the forthcoming show in Australia.
The 49-year-old, from Swansea, said she had her sights on becoming the first Welsh Queen of the Jungle.
"You makes Barry very proud, I'm not gonna lie," said Jones - assuming her former Gavin & Stacey character Nessa Jenkins - on Instagram.

articles.title: Irma P. Hall, Actress in ‘Soul Food’ and ‘The Ladykillers,’ Dies at 91
articles.summary: A Dallas schoolteacher for nearly three decades, she also appeared in ‘A Family Thing,’ ‘Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil’ and ‘Hap and Leonard.’
body: Irma P. Hall, the late-blooming actress known for portraying no-nonsense matriarchs in Soul Food and the Coen brothers’ adaptation of The Ladykillers, has died. She was 91.

Hall died Tuesday, her family announced, calling her “a beloved actress, author, poet, educator and public speaker whose contributions touched countless lives throughout her remarkable career. Her legacy of talent, dedication and compassion will continue to inspire generations to come.”

She also was a preacher in Daniel Petrie’s Square Dance (1987), a nurse in Ron Howard’s Backdraft (1991), a voodoo priestess in Clint Eastwood’s Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil (1997) and the domineering mother of Jamie Foxx’s character in Michael Mann’s Collateral (2004).
More recently, she made an impression as the wise, pie-making neighbor Meemaw on the Sundance TV series Hap and Leonard.
